title: Most Careers Stall at Mid-Level, No Matter How Long People Work ng-people-work
author: Ana Elena Azpurua
summary: This Working Knowledge piece reports on Paul Gompers and colleagues, who mined 150 million resumes to build an alternative yardstick for career attainment. Their complaint is that wages and job titles both mislead, the first because pay structures differ wildly across sectors and the second because title inflation is cheap to manufacture. Their proposed measure is a seniority level, defined as the median time it takes to reach a given title in an industry after entering the labour force, which lets progression be compared across companies and even across the government, nonprofit and private sectors. The headline finding is deflating: most people plateau at mid-level within fifteen to twenty years regardless of how long they keep working. The researchers illustrate the measure with Jerome Powell, whose move to a think tank salary of one dollar would read as a demotion on wages alone but registers correctly on seniority. The piece is a research digest rather than an argument, but it hands leaders a concrete instrument for thinking about progression.
points: Gompers and coauthors define seniority level as the median time to reach a title after entering the labour force, giving a non-wage measure of attainment.
The analysis draws on 150 million resumes plus wage data, and the underlying paper was released by the NBER in September 2025.
More than half of people with ten years of work data reached a seniority level of ten or higher, but only 19 percent of those with twenty years reached twenty.
The Jerome Powell example shows why wages alone mismeasure careers, since a one dollar salary at a think tank reads as a demotion but not on seniority.
The authors argue the measure is robust to fake promotions and title inflation that carry little economic value.
quotes: Many managers dream of reaching the C-suite, but most people's careers plateau at mid-level regardless of how long they work or how much they earn.

This uncomfortable reality is among the findings of an analysis of 150 million resumes by Harvard Business School Professor Paul Gompers that shows the limits of using wages and titles to gauge career attainment.
Gompers and fellow researchers mined resumes and wage data to calculate the median time to reach a given title in an industry—steps they call "seniority levels.

Exceptional workers will advance faster and achieve higher seniority earlier in their careers," Gompers writes in the working paper "Assessing Career Attainment via a Non-Wage Measure," released by the National Bureau of Economic Research in September 2025.

The team says that using seniority levels can be especially useful for assessing transitions across government, nonprofit, and private sector jobs with different pay structures. Seniority levels also predicted higher wages when people switch to new jobs.
Unlike Powell, most people top out much lower in the corporate pyramid, usually within 15-20 years into their careers.
The seniority measure avoids the problem of fake promotions or title inflation where the change in job title carries little economic value," the authors write.
